items.title: Thomas More's 'Utopia' (1516) coined the word
items.claim: What did Thomas More publish in 1516?

options.text: A history of the Wars of the Roses

'Utopia' — a Latin work describing a fictional island society, coining the word from Greek 'ou-topos' (no place) and 'eu-topos' (good place); a humanist critique of European politics, property and religion
A defence of the medieval feudal system

items.reveal_title: No place that critiques every place
items.reveal:
'Utopia' was written in Latin and first printed at Louvain in 1516. The Utopians hold property in common, work six hours a day, practise religious toleration and choose elected officials. The book mixes serious proposal with deliberate ambiguity — More may or may not endorse his fictional society.

More was Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII from 1529 to 1532, resigning over the king's annulment plans. He refused the Oath of Succession (1534) and was executed on 6 July 1535 with the famous 'King's good servant, but God's first.'

He was canonised in 1935. The word 'utopia' entered every European language as a term for an imagined ideal society.
items.why: Renaissance humanism produced political ideas centuries ahead of their reception. 'Utopia' has been read by socialists, anarchists, Catholics and modern progressives — each finding their own programme in More's deliberately ambiguous text.

items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: The US Vietnam draft was decided by a televised lottery
items.claim: How was the Vietnam draft (Selective Service) administered after 1969?

options.text: Strict order by date of birth, alphabetical
On 1 December 1969, blue capsules with birthdates were drawn from a glass jar on national TV — men born on dates drawn first were called up first
By state quota with each state choosing its own method

items.reveal:
The 1 December 1969 lottery selected 19-26 year olds. 366 capsules (one per birthday including 29 February) were drawn live. Men with low numbers (1-195) were called; high numbers (typically 196+) were spared.

The statistical method was later shown to have biased the draw — capsules added in order from January were less thoroughly mixed, so December birthdays were over-represented at low numbers.

Deferments before 1969 — for university students, for medical reasons — disproportionately spared the wealthy. Around 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam; 58,220 died. The draft ended in 1973.
items.why: Even apparently neutral mechanisms encode injustice. The Vietnam draft's class bias before 1969, and the statistical bias of the 1969 lottery itself, are case studies in how 'fairness' breaks down in practice.
